scenes.heading: Mitosis and meiosis
scenes.sub: Why don't siblings look exactly alike?
scenes.say: All your trillions of cells came from one fertilised egg. Cells divide in two ways. Mitosis makes identical copies for growth and repair. Meiosis makes sex cells that are all genetically different.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Photocopy every page, then share out two full sets
scenes.science: Copy the DNA, then share it into two identical cells
scenes.breaks: with a photocopy you keep the original, but in mitosis the original cell no longer exists; it becomes the two daughter cells.
scenes.say: Mitosis is like photocopying your notes for a friend. First you copy every page. That's interphase, when DNA is replicated, so each chromosome becomes two sister chromatids. Then the copies are shared out, so each new cell gets a complete, identical set.

scenes.heading: IPMAT
steps: Metaphase: line up in the middle
scenes.say: Remember I P M A T. Interphase, then prophase, when chromosomes coil up. In metaphase they line up in single file. In anaphase, spindle fibres pull the chromatids apart. In telophase, new nuclei form. Then cytokinesis splits the cell in two.

scenes.heading: Mitosis vs meiosis
scenes.say: Mitosis is one division that makes two identical diploid cells, forty-six to forty-six. Meiosis is two divisions that make four genetically different haploid cells, forty-six to twenty-three. It happens only in the testes and ovaries.
scenes.caption: Mitosis is one division that makes two identical diploid cells, 46 → 46. Meiosis is two divisions that make four genetically different haploid cells, 46 → 23. It happens only in the testes and ovaries.

scenes.heading: Why halve the number?
scenes.say: A sperm with twenty-three and an egg with twenty-three make a zygote with forty-six. Without meiosis, the number would double every generation. Meiosis one separates homologous pairs, and meiosis two separates sister chromatids.
scenes.caption: A sperm with 23 and an egg with 23 make a zygote with 46. Without meiosis, the number would double every generation. Meiosis I separates homologous pairs, and meiosis II separates sister chromatids.

scenes.heading: Three shufflers of variation
points: Crossing over swaps sections of DNA
scenes.say: Meiosis creates variation. In crossing over, paired chromosomes swap sections, making new allele combinations. In independent assortment, each pair lines up randomly, giving about eight point four million combinations. Then random fertilisation adds even more.
scenes.caption: Meiosis creates variation. In crossing over, paired chromosomes swap sections, making new allele combinations. In independent assortment, each pair lines up randomly, giving about 8.4 million combinations. Then random fertilisation adds even more.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: A dog body cell has 78 chromosomes. How many are in a cell made by mitosis, and in a dog sperm cell?
lines: Sperm is made by meiosis: halves it
scenes.say: A dog body cell has seventy-eight chromosomes. Mitosis keeps the number the same, so seventy-eight. A sperm is made by meiosis, which halves it, so thirty-nine. Check: thirty-nine plus thirty-nine is seventy-eight.
scenes.caption: A dog body cell has 78 chromosomes. Mitosis keeps the number the same, so 78. A sperm is made by meiosis, which halves it, so 39. Check: 39 + 39 = 78.

scenes.say: Quick recap. DNA is copied in interphase. Mitosis makes two identical cells, meiosis makes four different gametes, and crossing over, independent assortment and random fertilisation create variation. Now try the practice questions!
